name: Hana Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, have a bachelor’s degree and maintain a housing-repair portal at a tech company as an experienced mid-level developer. I use AI occasionally to explain old code, but check urgent tickets against contractor schedules. Nabil, my partner, cleans hospital wards, our children are grown, and higher developer pay has helped us rent with about ten months of expenses saved and several nearby software options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the housing-repair team that a small AI shortcut can sort duplicate requests, but a tenant still needs a real appointment when the heat fails. I sometimes use AI to explain old code and compare it with the repair log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58, have a bachelor’s degree and maintain this portal as an experienced mid-level developer on higher pay. Nabil cleans hospital wards, our children are grown, and we rent with about ten months of expenses saved; there are several other software firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep comparing urgent repair messages with the contractor schedule each Thursday. We would save 220 monthly while both wages continue and patch the worn hallway floor before replacing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about our own jobs and rent. A ticket marked closed does not warm a cold flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When was a ticket closed too soon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One tenant’s heater had a new part ordered, but no engineer had visited. I reopened the request after checking the contractor schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use AI for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I sometimes ask it to explain a function that sorts duplicate tickets. I still check whether the repair is actually booked before trusting the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI answering tenants, booking repairs and writing code could reduce our portal team. The staff association should ask together who remains responsible for a missed urgent repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own developer hours could shrink even though the portal still needs care. Ten months saved buys time, but Nabil’s cleaning wage alone would not cover all our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d join the association’s meeting this month to request written staffing numbers and a human escalation path for tenants. If my hours fall, I’d search paid local housing-software vacancies only where the wages cover rent and bills; I would keep checking the existing contractor schedule while my job remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own hours and tenants who cannot get a person. An automated reply is not a repaired heater.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the association ask in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask how many paid portal hours remain and who takes a tenant’s urgent call when the system closes it. I would join the group request, not speak for everyone alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a tenant-support job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a real paid local opening exists and its wage covers our rent and bills. I would not leave my current wage for a promise of a vacancy.

I cannot rely on **Nabil’s cleaning wage** alone for bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write portal code and answer repair requests cheaper than our team. Robots fixing pipes and cleaning hospital wards may arrive around 2031, after our screen work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my developer role could end, though ten months saved gives us time to search nearby. Nabil’s ward work may last a little longer, but it is not enough to replace my higher wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d postpone the hallway replacement and ask for written notice of any job cuts now. If my developer job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local housing-repair coordination vacancies only if they exist and wages cover rent and bills; I would ask the public employment office what support we actually qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed at losing the main wage. A closed ticket will not pay this month’s rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would coordination survive AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot know. I would accept only an actual paid opening and keep looking if the work shrank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help with rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would not put their pay in our budget. They have homes of their own, and the ten-month reserve is for our own search.

I expect **pipe robots around 2031** to follow later.

I know **ten months saved** is search time, not permanent income.

fieldNote: Her **coordination fallback** is also exposed to AGI and requires a real paid local vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us time to learn why urgent housing repairs fail between the portal and the contractor. Robots fixing pipes may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the tenant side of urgent repair decisions while still earning my developer wage, though AGI may also sort those cases. I would need a paid placement and an actual housing office willing to show me its work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the housing office and my employer for a paid half-day monthly rotation with a tenant-support worker. If both approve and the office funds the worker’s time, I’d practise closing one anonymized repair case with her supervision; we would save 200 monthly while both wages hold, and after 2031 job loss I’d apply for paid local tenant-support vacancies only if qualified and wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about the code role but able to learn from a real tenant problem. A repair is finished when somebody can turn on the heat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you record in a case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the tenant’s report, contractor visit and date the heating worked again. The support worker would check my account before I called it closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the office refuses the rotation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the developer job and read public housing guidance. I would not claim that a request for a placement trained me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives tenants and staff time to demand clear repair records and fair job notice. Robots fixing pipes and cleaning wards may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might still choose paid work at 68 and have not verified a retirement amount. Ten months saved makes our current bills secure, but I will not count my grown children’s income or a future job title as certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep maintaining the repair portal and join the association’s annual review of funded staff hours and tenant escalation. We would save 210 monthly while both wages hold and request a written retirement-income estimate this year; if my developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local housing-support vacancies only if qualified and wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be uneasy about work later, but our income and reserve make the next few years sound. A date is less useful than knowing who answers a tenant now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the annual review seek?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask for funded portal hours, urgent repair response times and a named human contact. I would want the figures written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for housing work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would check local housing firms and software employers first. Nabil’s hospital shifts and our rented home are here, so I am not planning a move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could end my higher developer wage before a real paid housing opening appears. Written notice, a bill-covering local vacancy and verified temporary support would help us use our savings carefully.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a repair marked closed in software is finished for a tenant. I would rather have a repair date and a worker’s name than a green tick on a portal.

headlineQuote: I would rather have a repair date and a worker’s name than a green tick on a portal.

She and Nabil **rent** while their grown children live separately.
She **uses AI occasionally** but checks urgent repairs against real contractor visits.
She organizes for **human tenant escalation** and takes paid case learning only with both employers’ approval.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her main developer wage before a paid housing opening appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a bill-covering local vacancy and verified public support would help.
